final_text: DynamoDB's maximum item size is 400 KB, including attribute names, so a single item cannot hold a 4 MB value; large binary values must live elsewhere (AWS suggests S3) with a reference stored in the item.
note: Opened Constraints: 'The maximum item size in DynamoDB is 400 KB, which includes both attribute name binary length (UTF-8 length) and attribute value lengths'. The 'live elsewhere' half is not on that page; I added bp-use-s3-too (opened): 'store the item as an object in Amazon S3 and store the Amazon S3 object identifier in your DynamoDB item'.

final_text: CAP 'consistency' means linearizability: if a read starts after a write completes, it must see that write or a newer one. A database can be ACID (serializable or snapshot isolation) and still not be linearizable.
note: Opened Kleppmann (2015): 'Consistency in CAP actually means linearizability'; 'If operation B started after operation A successfully completed, then operation B must see the the system in the same state as it was on completion of operation A, or a newer state'; 'PostgreSQL's SSI provides serializability but not linearizability'; 'Just because a database is branded ACID doesn't mean it meets the CAP theorem's definition of consistency.' Author of DDIA; reputable secondary source.

final_text: DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default; setting ConsistentRead=true returns the latest committed data on tables and local secondary indexes, at twice the read cost. Reads from global secondary indexes are always eventually consistent.
note: Opened: 'eventually consistent (default)'; 'If you set ConsistentRead to true, DynamoDB returns a response with the most up-to-date data'; 'Strongly consistent reads are only supported on tables and local secondary indexes'; 'Eventually consistent reads are half the cost of strongly consistent reads'; 'All reads from GSIs and streams are eventually consistent'.

final_text: In DynamoDB each partition has three replicas in different Availability Zones; the leader acknowledges a write once a quorum (two of the three) has persisted the log record.
note: WebFetch saved the PDF as binary; I extracted its text locally (zlib-inflated content streams, read-only). USENIX ATC'22 paper: 'A write is acknowledged to the application once a quorum of peers persists the log record to their local write-ahead logs'; s6.1: 'A healthy write quorum in the case of DynamoDB consists of two out of the three replicas from different AZs.' Paper is dated 2022; describes the design at that time.

final_text: PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default, so committed transactions can be lost if the primary crashes before the standby receives them; synchronous replication makes each commit wait for a standby's confirmation.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 docs 26.2.8: 'PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default'; 'some transactions that were committed may not have been replicated to the standby server, causing data loss'; synchronous: 'each commit of a write transaction will wait until confirmation is received'.

final_text: Vitess is an open-source clustering system that shards MySQL across many instances while applications query it as one database; it served all YouTube database traffic for over five years.
note: Opened vitess.io: 'open-source database clustering system for horizontal scaling of MySQL'; 'Vitess served all YouTube database traffic for over five years'.

final_text: Redis Cluster splits keys over 16384 hash slots and implements all single-key commands, but multi-key operations work only when all keys hash to the same slot; 'hash tags' let you force related keys into one slot.
note: Opened Redis cluster spec: 'The cluster's key space is split into 16384 slots'; 'Redis Cluster implements all the single key commands'; hash tags 'force certain keys to be stored in the same hash slot'; multi-key ops limited to keys in the same slot.

final_text: A DynamoDB filter expression is applied after the Query has read the items, so it consumes the same read capacity as without the filter; to query efficiently by a non-key attribute you need a secondary index.
note: Opened: 'A filter expression is applied after a Query finishes, but before the results are returned. Therefore, a Query consumes the same amount of read capacity, regardless of whether a filter expression is present.' The secondary-index clause is standard guidance, not on this page (the page says to avoid queries that discard most items).

final_text: Redis hashes allow field-level updates: HSET sets individual fields of the hash stored at a key without rewriting the other fields.
note: Opened: 'Sets the specified fields to their respective values in the hash stored at key. This command overwrites the values of specified fields that exist in the hash.'

final_text: MongoDB's documentation says a distributed transaction 'incurs a greater performance cost over single document writes' and should not replace effective schema design; single-document operations are always atomic, so embedding related data often avoids transactions.
note: Opened MongoDB 9.0 manual: 'In most cases, a distributed transaction incurs a greater performance cost over single document writes, and the availability of distributed transactions should not be a replacement for effective schema design'; 'an operation on a single document is atomic'; embedded documents mean 'multi-document transactions are not necessary for many practical use cases'.

final_text: Redshift's docs give the arithmetic: in a 100-column table, a query using five columns reads only about five percent of the data, while a row-wise database would also read the blocks holding the 95 unneeded columns.
note: Opened: 'suppose a table contains 100 columns. A query that uses five columns will only need to read about five percent of the data'; 'a row-wise database would read the blocks that contain the 95 unneeded columns as well'.

final_text: Columnar is a storage layout, not a NoSQL category: BigQuery and Redshift are SQL warehouses that store each column separately. 'Wide-column' stores such as Cassandra are a different idea.
note: Opened BigQuery storage overview: 'BigQuery stores table data in columnar format, meaning it stores each column separately.' Redshift: columnar storage is 'the method Amazon Redshift uses to store tabular data'. The Cassandra contrast is not sourced on these pages; it is a standard distinction.

final_text: Parquet's dictionary encoding builds a dictionary of the values in a column and stores small codes instead; repeated values are then packed with run-length encoding plus bit-packing.
note: Opened: 'The dictionary encoding builds a dictionary of values encountered in a given column'; indices 'stored as integers using the RLE/Bit-Packing Hybrid encoding'.

final_text: ClickHouse recommends inserting in batches of at least 1,000 rows, ideally 10,000-100,000, because each synchronous insert immediately creates a new storage part on disk; async inserts let the server do the batching instead.
note: Opened: 'We recommend inserting data in batches of at least 1,000 rows, and ideally between 10,000-100,000 rows'; 'Each insert query immediately creates a storage part on disk, including metadata and indexes'; async inserts 'shift batching responsibility from the client to the server'. I did not find the 'background merges may fall behind' wording in what I read, so I replaced it with the page's own reason.

final_text: BigQuery on-demand pricing bills queries by the number of bytes read, with capacity (slot) pricing as the reserved alternative; Redshift Serverless bills for compute actually used, with optional reservations.
note: Opened estimate-costs: 'When using the on-demand pricing model, queries are billed according to the number of bytes read'; capacity compute charges for compute resources via reservations. Redshift Serverless: 'You can purchase on-demand capacity ... you pay for resources as you go'; 'You can purchase reservations'; minimum 60 s, per-second metering.

final_text: PostgreSQL's WITH RECURSIVE lets a query refer to its own output and is 'typically used to deal with hierarchical or tree-structured data', so arbitrary-depth traversal needs one query, not one join per level.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 docs: 'Using RECURSIVE, a WITH query can refer to its own output'; 'Recursive queries are typically used to deal with hierarchical or tree-structured data'.

final_text: Twitter stored its social graph (who follows whom, who blocks whom) in FlockDB, which kept adjacency lists and explicitly listed multi-hop graph-walking queries as a non-goal.
note: Opened README: 'Twitter uses FlockDB to store social graphs (who follows whom, who blocks whom) and secondary indices'; 'a distributed graph database for storing adjancency lists' (sic); non-goals: 'multi-hop queries (or graph-walking queries)'. Archived project: historical.

final_text: Amazon's recommender moved to item-to-item collaborative filtering: item B is related to A if buyers of A are unusually likely to buy B, and related-item lists for every product are recomputed daily.
note: Opened Amazon Science: 'item B is related to item A if purchasers of A are more likely to buy B than the average Amazon customer is'; 'computationally feasible to produce an updated list of related items for every product on the Amazon site on a daily basis'. No graph database is mentioned.

final_text: Amazon Neptune has a single primary instance that performs all writes, plus up to 15 read replicas sharing a storage volume replicated across Availability Zones.
note: Opened Neptune intro: 'Each Neptune DB cluster has one primary DB instance that is responsible for writing'; 'up to 15 Neptune Replicas'; replicas 'Connects to the same storage volume'; 'A cluster volume consists of copies of the data across multiple Availability Zones'.

final_text: Kafka does not delete events when they are consumed; a topic keeps them for its configured retention period and they can be read as often as needed, so consumers can rewind and reprocess.
note: Opened kafka.apache.org/intro: 'Events in a topic can be read as often as needed'; 'events are not deleted after consumption'; retention 'through a per-topic configuration setting'.

final_text: CockroachDB is a concrete case of the NAND-gate idea: its SQL layer converts SQL statements into key-value operations over a sorted key-value map split into ranges.
note: Opened: CockroachDB 'converts clients' SQL statements into key-value (KV) data'; 'stores all user data ... in a sorted map of key-value pairs. This keyspace is divided into contiguous chunks called ranges'.

final_text: microservices.io lists database-per-service benefits (schema changes do not affect other services; each service picks the best store) and shared-database drawbacks (schema-change coordination, services interfering at runtime).
note: Opened both: 'Changes to one service's database does not impact any other services'; 'Each service can use the type of database that is best suited to its needs'; shared DB: 'coordinate schema changes with the developers of other services'; services 'can potentially interfere with one another' (lock example).

final_text: Cassandra's commit log logs every write made to a node, giving durable writes even after an unexpected shutdown; its append-only LSM design is what makes heavy ingestion cheap.
note: Opened: 'When a write operation takes place, Cassandra records the data in a local append-only commit log on disk'; it 'provides permanent durable writes'; protects writes 'If an unexpected shutdown occurs'; engine built on 'Log Structured Merge (LSM) trees'. 'Cheap ingestion' is an inference from append-only writes.

final_text: Redis can persist with RDB snapshots (on by default) or an append-only file (AOF, turned on with appendonly yes); with AOF's default fsync-every-second policy you can lose about one second of writes on a crash.
note: Opened redis.io persistence: RDB 'point-in-time snapshots'; 'By default Redis saves snapshots of the dataset on disk'; AOF enabled with 'appendonly yes'; 'The suggested (and default) policy is to fsync every second'; 'you can only lose one second worth of writes'. Original wording implied AOF itself is the default; it is not, only its fsync policy is.

final_text: In Slack's API every channel-like thing is a conversation: public channel, private channel, DM (is_im) or multi-person DM (is_mpim). conversations.open opens or resumes a DM and returns its channel ID; chat.postMessage can also take a user ID and opens the DM if needed.
note: Opened all three: is_im 'direct message between two distinguished individuals or a user and a bot', is_mpim 'unnamed private conversation between multiple users'; conversations.open 'Opens or resumes a direct message or multi-person direct message', returns channel id; chat.postMessage: 'provide the user's ID as the channel value and a direct message conversation will be opened if it isn't open already'.

final_text: Slack exposes exactly this checkpoint: the conversation object's last_read is 'the timestamp for the last message the calling user has read in this channel', and conversations.mark moves that read cursor to a given message ts.
note: Opened: last_read 'The timestamp for the last message the calling user has read in this channel'; conversations.mark 'Sets the read cursor in a channel'; ts 'Unique identifier of message you want marked as most recently seen'. Quote matches (case aside).

final_text: If you do keep two either/or columns, the database can still forbid orphan rows: PostgreSQL's num_nonnulls() lets a CHECK constraint require exactly one of channel_id and receiver_id to be set.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 Table 9.3: num_nonnulls 'Returns the number of non-null arguments'. The page has no CHECK-constraint example; CHECK (num_nonnulls(channel_id, receiver_id) = 1) is a valid application (CHECK constraints accept any boolean expression), not a quote.

final_text: Slack has used MySQL for all its data from the beginning, originally partitioned by workspace id. From 2017 it migrated to Vitess (sharded MySQL), which by 2020 served 99% of its query load at about 2.3 million queries per second at peak.
note: Opened Slack Engineering (1 Dec 2020): 'From the very beginning of Slack, MySQL was used as the storage engine for all our data'; 'partitioned and scaled horizontally by workspace id'; 'Our migration to Vitess began in 2017 and Vitess now serves 99% of our overall query load'; 'Today, we serve 2.3 million QPS at peak.'

final_text: Slack's original sharding by workspace kept each workspace on one shard. In moving to Vitess the team wanted to shard message data by channel id to spread load more evenly, the same key the lecture uses.
note: Opened: 'we wanted to shard the message data by the unique id of the channel. This would spread the load around much more evenly.' Correctly says 'wanted'; the post does not state the migration's final shard key as completed.

final_text: Discord stored its messages in Cassandra (12 nodes and billions of messages in 2017) and moved them to ScyllaDB, a Cassandra-compatible database, in May 2022. Messages are partitioned by channel and a time bucket.
note: Opened Discord blog: 'In 2017, we ran 12 Cassandra nodes, storing billions of messages'; ScyllaDB 'a Cassandra-compatible database written in C++'; 'We switched our messages database over in May 2022'; 'We partition our messages by the channel they're sent in, along with a bucket, which is a static time window.'

final_text: With Cassandra the schema does change shape: modelling is query-driven, joins are not supported, and data is denormalised into one table per query, with a partition key that decides which node holds the data.
note: Opened: 'data modeling is query-driven'; 'joins are not supported in Cassandra'; 'data is duplicated across multiple tables in a process known as denormalization'; 'A partition key is used to partition data among the nodes'.

final_text: Browsers count WebSockets separately from ordinary HTTP connections. Chromium allows 6 normal sockets per host but 255 WebSockets per host ('WebSocket connections are long-lived, and should be treated differently'), and Firefox's network.websocket.max-connections is 200.
note: Opened the cited Chromium 125.0.6422.5 tag (6 / 255, 'Use a limit of 255', 'Firefox uses a limit of 200') and also Chromium main (same values, '6, // kNormal', '255 // kWebSocket', and the quoted comment), so I switched the source to main to show it is current as of 2026-10-13. Firefox all.js (mozilla-firefox/firefox main): pref('network.websocket.max-connections', 200); pref('network.http.max-persistent-connections-per-server', 6).

final_text: HTTP/2 runs many concurrent streams over a single connection, so on HTTP/2 sites the six-per-host cap does not throttle requests. RFC 8441 also lets a WebSocket run over a single stream of an HTTP/2 connection.
note: Opened RFC 9113 s5: 'A single HTTP/2 connection can contain multiple concurrently open streams'. RFC 8441 abstract: 'mechanism for running the WebSocket Protocol over a single stream of an HTTP/2 connection'.

final_text: Redis Pub/Sub delivery is at-most-once: if a subscriber errors or disconnects, the message is lost forever. When a missed message matters, Redis Streams persist messages and support at-least-once delivery.
note: Opened: 'Redis' Pub/Sub exhibits at-most-once message delivery semantics'; 'due to an error or a network disconnect) the message is forever lost'; 'Messages in streams are persisted, and support both at-most-once as well as at-least-once delivery semantics.'

final_text: Since Redis 7.0, sharded Pub/Sub (SSUBSCRIBE/SPUBLISH) assigns channels to cluster slots like keys and keeps each message within its shard. Classic PUBLISH in a cluster goes to every node, so only sharded Pub/Sub scales horizontally by adding shards.
note: Opened: 'From Redis 7.0, sharded Pub/Sub is introduced in which shard channels are assigned to slots by the same algorithm used to assign keys to slots'; 'restricts the propagation of messages to be within the shard'; global Pub/Sub 'each message propagates to each node in the cluster'; 'horizontally scale the Pub/Sub usage by adding more shards'.

final_text: This is what Socket.IO's Redis adapter does: it broadcasts packets between multiple Socket.IO servers through Redis Pub/Sub (a sharded variant needs Redis 7.0+). The adapter does not sign, encrypt or authenticate these messages, so Redis must stay inside trusted infrastructure.
note: Opened README: 'allows broadcasting packets between multiple Socket.IO servers'; sharded adapter requires Redis 7.0; 'Messages exchanged through Redis Pub/Sub are not signed, encrypted, or authenticated by the adapter'; Redis should not be exposed to untrusted networks.

final_text: Slack's published architecture differs in detail: stateful, in-memory Channel Servers own channels via consistent hashing (about 16 million channels per host at peak), and Gateway Servers hold users' WebSocket subscriptions and subscribe to those Channel Servers. Slack reports delivering messages across the world in 500 ms.
note: Opened Slack Engineering (11 Apr 2023): 'Every CS is mapped to a subset of channels based on consistent hashing'; 'about 16 million channels are served per host' at peak and 'tens of millions of channels per host'; 'our system delivers messages across the world in 500ms'. Replaced 'millions' with the page's figure and dropped 'about' from 500 ms.

final_text: In Slack, the client first gets its token and connection details from the web app backend, then opens a WebSocket to the nearest edge region. There an Envoy proxy forwards it to a Gateway Server, which loads the user's channels and subscribes to them.
note: Opened: 'On boot up, the client fetches the user token and websocket connection setup information from the Webapp backend'; 'A client initiates a websocket connection to the nearest edge region'; Envoy forwards to the Gateway Server, which fetches 'the user information, including all the user's channels, from Webapp' and subscribes.

final_text: Slack terminates WebSocket connections on proxies in multiple regions close to users (HAProxy, replaced globally by Envoy) and forwards them to its backend WebSocket services.
note: Opened Slack Engineering (15 Mar 2021, updated 21 Jun 2021): HAProxy instances in several regions 'terminate websocket connections close to the user' and 'forward the request to corresponding backend services'; 'the entire HAProxy websocket stack was replaced with Envoy Proxy globally'; backend is 'wss' (WebSocket Service).

final_text: Kafka can authenticate client connections (SSL or SASL) and authorise read/write operations per client. An edge server can therefore get a credential limited to writing one topic, so a breach exposes as little as possible.
note: Checker cited /42/, which now says 'You are viewing documentation for an older version (4.2)'. Opened the 4.3 page (current): 'Authentication of connections to brokers from clients ... using either SSL or SASL'; 'Authorization of read / write operations by clients'. Same text; source switched to 4.3. The least-privilege sentence is an application, not a quote.

final_text: OWASP classes this as broken access control (A01 in both the 2021 and the current 2025 Top 10): users acting outside their intended permissions, e.g. by tampering with a request parameter. The recommended baseline is 'except for public resources, deny by default', so membership must be checked server-side.
note: Opened A01:2021: 'users cannot act outside of their intended permissions'; 'Bypassing access control checks by modifying the URL (parameter tampering or force browsing)'; 'Except for public resources, deny by default'. top10.owasp.org now redirects to 'OWASP Top 10:2025', where A01 is 'Broken Access Control' (opened); added the edition note so the page does not cite only a superseded list.

final_text: The most common DDoS attacks (UDP reflection, SYN floods) are infrastructure-layer floods. Mitigating them requires network capacity that scales faster than the attack, to filter or absorb it, which an application rate limiter cannot provide.
note: Opened AWS whitepaper: 'The most common DDoS attacks, User Datagram Protocol (UDP) reflection attacks and SYN floods, are infrastructure layer attacks'; 'you must have a network or systems that scale up capacity more rapidly than the inbound traffic flood' to 'filter out or absorb the attack traffic'. The rate-limiter clause is an inference.

final_text: An L4 load balancer such as AWS NLB picks a target by flow hash, and 'each individual TCP connection is routed to a single target for the life of the connection'. A WebSocket through it is therefore pinned to one server without terminating the connection at the load balancer.
note: Opened NLB intro: 'the load balancer selects a target using a flow hash algorithm'; 'Each individual TCP connection is routed to a single target for the life of the connection.' 'Without terminating' holds for plain TCP listeners (TLS listeners do terminate TLS); acceptable as stated.

final_text: WebTransport sends data over HTTP/3 with multiple streams, unidirectional streams and unreliable UDP-like datagrams. MDN lists it as Baseline 2026, working across the latest major browsers since March 2026 (checked 2026-10-12).
note: Opened MDN (last modified 25 Sep 2026): 'using HTTP/3 Transport'; 'support for multiple streams, unidirectional streams, and out-of-order delivery'; 'unreliable transport via UDP-like datagrams'; 'Baseline 2026 / Newly available ... Since March 2026, this feature works across the latest devices and browser versions.' Re-checked 2026-10-13.

final_text: Redis Pub/Sub has at-most-once delivery: if a subscriber is disconnected or fails to handle a message, that message is lost for good. Redis Streams persist messages and support at-least-once delivery when that is needed.
note: Opened redis.io Pub/Sub; same quotes as A-SRW-10 ('at-most-once', 'forever lost', Streams 'persisted'). Optional because it duplicates A-SRW-10 on a neighbouring item; keep one on the page.

final_text: Since Redis 7.0, sharded Pub/Sub (SSUBSCRIBE/SPUBLISH) keeps a message within one shard of a cluster; classic Pub/Sub propagates every message to every node, which limits how far it scales.
note: Opened; same quotes as A-SRW-11 ('restricts the propagation of messages to be within the shard'; 'each message propagates to each node in the cluster'). Optional: duplicate of A-SRW-11.

final_text: Slack's own description (April 2023): the client sends a message by calling Slack's Webapp API; a Channel Server chosen by consistent hashing on the channel fans it out to every Gateway Server subscribed to that channel, and Gateway Servers, deployed in multiple regions, hold the clients' WebSocket connections.
note: Opened Slack Engineering (11 Apr 2023): 'the client hits our Webapp API to send a message'; consistent hashing for Channel Servers; GSs 'deployed across multiple geographical regions'. The post does not say 'HTTP'; the public Web API is HTTP ('POST https://slack.com/api/chat.postMessage', opened), so the HTTP link is supported via that page, but 'HTTP Webapp API' was reworded to avoid attributing it to the post. Overlaps A-SRW-13/A-SRW-14 (same post); keep this one for the send-over-HTTP point.

final_text: Slack's 2020 Vitess post explains that its original databases were sharded by workspace id, and that with Vitess it wanted to shard message data by channel id because that spreads the load much more evenly.
note: Opened: 'partitioned and scaled horizontally by workspace id'; 'we wanted to shard the message data by the unique id of the channel. This would spread the load around much more evenly.' Wording already correctly says 'wanted'. Optional: duplicates A-SRW-05 (same source and point).

final_text: WhatsApp deletes messages from its servers once delivered; an undelivered message is held encrypted on its servers for up to 30 days while delivery is retried, then deleted.
note: Opened WhatsApp privacy policy (effective 4 Jan 2021): 'Once your messages are delivered, they are deleted from our servers'; undelivered: 'we keep it in encrypted form on our servers for up to 30 days as we try to deliver it'.

final_text: Alternatives to WebSocket for receiving: Server-Sent Events give a one-way server-to-client stream over HTTP, and HTTP long polling holds the request open until there is new data. Short polling is what gives the poor real-time UX.
note: Opened MDN SSE: 'This is a one-way connection, so you can't send events from a client to a server'; server responds with 'text/event-stream'. RFC 6202 (2011, Informational): server attempts to 'hold open (not immediately reply to) each HTTP request', 'responding only when there are events to deliver'.

final_text: HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default, so repeated REST calls usually reuse one TCP/TLS connection instead of handshaking each time.
note: Opened RFC 9112 9.3: 'HTTP/1.1 defaults to the use of "persistent connections"'.

final_text: QUIC, the transport under HTTP/3, runs over UDP datagrams and builds its own reliable delivery and congestion control on top. UDP itself guarantees nothing; reliability has to be added above it.
note: Opened RFC 9000: 'QUIC packets are carried in UDP datagrams'; 'QUIC provides the necessary feedback to implement reliable delivery and congestion control'. RFC 9000's opening does not mention HTTP/3, so I opened RFC 9114 and added it: 'This document describes a mapping of HTTP semantics over QUIC.'

final_text: Kafka consumers can reprocess records: if a consumer crashes after processing a batch but before saving its offset, its replacement reads them again. Writes keyed by a unique message id turn that redelivery into a harmless overwrite.
note: Opened Kafka 4.3 design: 'the consumer process crashes after processing messages but before saving its position'; 'This corresponds to the at-least-once semantics in the case of consumer failure.' Idempotent-write sentence is standard advice.

final_text: Kafka does not delete messages when they are consumed; it keeps them for a configured time- or size-based retention window, so consumers can re-read history within that window.
note: Opened Kafka 4.3 design: data 'discarded after a fixed period of time or when the log reaches some predetermined size'; 'This retention policy can be set per-topic'. Optional: overlaps A-DC-20.

final_text: Slack's message 'ts' value is essentially the message ID and is guaranteed unique within a channel or conversation, giving one server-assigned order per channel.
note: Opened: 'The ts value is essentially the ID of the message, guaranteed unique within the context of a channel or conversation.'

final_text: Zoom offers continuous meeting chat: when an admin enables it, in-meeting messages also appear in a persistent Team Chat group, so they live on before, during and after the meeting.
note: Opened Zoom blog (published 22 Jun 2023, updated June 2026): 'messages can live on after a meeting in our persistent chat solution'; setup step 'Enable continuous meeting chat'. The page does not say that without it participants see only messages sent while present, so that sentence was removed.

final_text: A vector clock holds one counter per process and gives a partial causal order: it can say message A happened before B, or that they were concurrent, but it does not by itself order concurrent messages.
note: Opened Wikipedia: 'a vector ... of n logical clocks, one clock per process'; 'Vector clocks allow for the partial causal ordering of events.' Concurrency detection follows from the comparison rules on the page.

final_text: WhatsApp completed its rollout of the Signal Protocol for end-to-end encryption in April 2016, covering one-to-one chats, group chats, attachments, voice notes and calls.
note: Opened Signal blog (05 Apr 2016): 'the integration is fully complete'; covers 'chats, group chats, attachments, voice notes, and voice calls'.

final_text: Apache Parquet is an open-source, column-oriented file format with compression and encoding schemes built for efficient bulk storage and retrieval, which is why warehouses and lakes favour it.
note: Opened: 'an open source, column-oriented data file format designed for efficient data storage and retrieval'; 'high performance compression and encoding schemes'.

final_text: In the 1945 EDVAC report von Neumann based his logic 'E elements' on the biological neuron, following McCulloch and Pitts' 1943 model, and built them as digital devices from one or two vacuum tubes.
note: Opened Wikipedia: E elements 'based on the biological neuron as model' (footnote cites McCulloch and Pitts 1943); constructed 'using one or two vacuum tubes'; 'digital devices'. Reworded to match: the article attributes the McCulloch-Pitts link via a footnote.
